findings.proposed_proof:
**Given:** The inherited $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [A1]; the curvature $k\in\mathbb R$ and dimension $n\ge2$; the model functions $\operatorname{sn}_k,\operatorname{cs}_k,\operatorname{ct}_k$ of [F1] with their ODE and Wronskian identities [F2]; for [F4] an admissible side datum $(a,b,c)$ in the sense of the comparison-triangle definition, its comparison angle $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ opposite the side $c$ between the sides $a$ and $b$, and the halves $s:=(a+b)/2$, $u:=(a-b)/2$, $v:=c/2$; for the hinge form a unit-speed model hinge with sides $a,b>0$ and included angle $\theta$; a point $p$ in the space form, a point $q$ off $p$ and off its cut locus with $t_0:=d_g(p,q)>0$, and a radius $r>0$.

[A1] The countable-choice premise is the inherited $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), carried by the comparison suppliers of this page. This example selects no family of objects: the model geodesics, Jacobi fields and comparison triangles it mentions are supplied by the cited definitions and theorems, and every computation below is performed on the explicit formulas.

[F1] Model functions ([[def-comparison-sine-cosine-and-cotangent-functions]]): $\operatorname{sn}_0(t)=t$, $\operatorname{sn}_k(t)=\sin(\sqrt k\,t)/\sqrt k$ for $k>0$ and $\operatorname{sn}_k(t)=\sinh(\sqrt{-k}\,t)/\sqrt{-k}$ for $k<0$; $\operatorname{cs}_k=\operatorname{sn}_k'$ is $1$, $\cos(\sqrt k\,t)$, $\cosh(\sqrt{-k}\,t)$ in the same three cases; $\operatorname{ct}_k=\operatorname{cs}_k/\operatorname{sn}_k$; $\operatorname{sn}_k$ is odd and $\operatorname{cs}_k$ is even. On the positive domain of $\operatorname{sn}_k$, $\operatorname{sn}_k>0$; $\operatorname{ct}_k>0$ for $k\le0$, while for $k>0$ it changes sign at $\pi/(2\sqrt k)$ within $(0,\pi/\sqrt k)$.

[F2] Model ODE and Wronskian ([[prop-model-functions-solve-the-constant-curvature-jacobi-equation]]): $\operatorname{sn}_k''+k\operatorname{sn}_k=0$, $\operatorname{cs}_k''+k\operatorname{cs}_k=0$, $\operatorname{cs}_k^2+k\operatorname{sn}_k^2=1$ on $\mathbb R$, with $\operatorname{sn}_k(0)=0$, $\operatorname{cs}_k(0)=1$, $\operatorname{sn}_k'(0)=1$, $\operatorname{cs}_k'(0)=0$.

[F3] Addition formulas ([[cor-complex-trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-addition-formulas]], [[thm-hyperbolic-identities-and-derivatives]]): the sine, cosine, hyperbolic sine and hyperbolic cosine addition formulas hold; consequently, for all real $x,y$ and all $k$, $$\operatorname{sn}_k(x+y)=\operatorname{sn}_k(x)\operatorname{cs}_k(y)+\operatorname{cs}_k(x)\operatorname{sn}_k(y),\qquad \operatorname{cs}_k(x\pm y)=\operatorname{cs}_k(x)\operatorname{cs}_k(y)\mp k\operatorname{sn}_k(x)\operatorname{sn}_k(y),$$ and $\operatorname{sn}_k(2x)=2\operatorname{sn}_k(x)\operatorname{cs}_k(x)$, $\operatorname{cs}_k(2x)=1-2k\operatorname{sn}_k(x)^2$. Moreover $(\cot x)'=-\csc^2x$ and $(\coth y)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2y$ on their domains ([[thm-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant-derivatives-and-periods]], the hyperbolic identities and derivatives theorem).

[F4] Model cosine law and comparison triangle ([[def-comparison-triangle-in-the-two-dimensional-space-form]]): for an admissible side datum $(a,b,c)$ in $M^2_k$ there is a comparison triangle, unique up to isometry of $M^2_k$, and its angle $\theta$ opposite the side $c$ between the sides $a$ and $b$ is determined by the model cosine law, which in the unified notation is $$\cos\theta=\frac{\operatorname{cs}_k(c)-\operatorname{cs}_k(a)\operatorname{cs}_k(b)}{k\operatorname{sn}_k(a)\operatorname{sn}_k(b)}$$ for $k\ne0$ and $\cos\theta=(a^2+b^2-c^2)/(2ab)$ for $k=0$. Admissibility means $a,b,c>0$, the strict triangle inequalities, and when $k>0$ also $a,b,c<\pi/\sqrt k$ and $a+b+c<2\pi/\sqrt k$; the angle lies in $(0,\pi)$.

[F5] Model Jacobi fields and Rauch comparison ([[ex-model-jacobi-fields-in-positive-zero-and-negative-curvature]], [[thm-rauch-comparison-theorem-first-form]]): in a space form of curvature $k$ the normal Jacobi field with $J(0)=0$, $D_tJ(0)=E$ is $J(t)=\operatorname{sn}_k(t)P_tE$; Rauch's theorem compares two manifolds with $\sec_{M_1}\ge\sec_{M_2}$ and gives $|J_1|\le|J_2|$ for matched initial data up to the first conjugate instant of $\gamma_1$.

[F6] Hessian comparison ([[thm-hessian-comparison-for-distance-under-sectional-curvature-bounds]]): at $q$ off $p$ and the cut locus, with $t_0<\pi/\sqrt k$ when $k>0$, the curvature bound $K\ge k$ along the minimizing geodesic gives $\operatorname{Hess}r\le\operatorname{ct}_k(t_0)g$ on the normal hyperplane, and the reverse curvature bound gives the reverse inequality.

[F7] Laplacian comparison ([[thm-laplacian-comparison-for-distance-under-a-ricci-lower-bound]]): $\operatorname{Ric}\ge(n-1)k\,g$ gives $\Delta_gr(q)\le(n-1)\operatorname{ct}_k(t_0)$.

[F8] Space-form equalities ([[ex-distance-hessian-and-laplacian-in-space-forms]]): in the space form of curvature $k$, $\operatorname{Hess}r=\operatorname{ct}_k(t_0)(g-dr\otimes dr)$ on all of $T_qM$ and $\Delta_gr(q)=(n-1)\operatorname{ct}_k(t_0)$; both comparison hypotheses of [F6] and [F7] hold with equality there.

[F9] Bishop–Gromov comparison and model volumes ([[thm-bishop-gromov-volume-comparison]], [[def-model-space-radial-area-and-ball-volume]], [[ex-bishop-gromov-ratio-is-constant-in-the-model-space]]): for $\operatorname{Ric}\ge(n-1)k\,g$ the ratio $R_p(r)=\operatorname{vol}_g(B(p,r))/V^\star_k(r)$ is nonincreasing with $\lim_{r\downarrow0}R_p(r)=1$; the model radial area is $A_k(t)=\omega_{n-1}\operatorname{sn}_k(t)^{n-1}$, the model ball volume is $V_k(r)=\int_0^rA_k$, and in the space form of curvature $k$, $\operatorname{vol}_g(B(p,r))=V^\star_k(r)$ for every $r>0$.

[F10] Toponogov hinge and triangle comparison ([[thm-toponogov-hinge-comparison]], [[thm-toponogov-triangle-comparison]]): $K\ge k$ gives $c\le c_k(a,b,\theta)$ for every admissible minimizing hinge, where $c_k(a,b,\theta)$ is the opposite side of the model hinge in $M^2_k$ determined by the cosine law of [F4]; and every actual angle of an admissible minimizing geodesic triangle is at least its comparison angle.

[F11] Taylor–Peano ([[thm-taylor-peano-remainder]]): a function that is $m$ times differentiable on an open neighborhood of $0$ has its order-$m$ Taylor expansion with remainder $o(x^m)$ there. In particular the smooth sine and hyperbolic sine satisfy $\sin x=x-x^3/6+o(x^3)$ and $\sinh x=x+x^3/6+o(x^3)$.



**Proof technique:** direct. The comparison coefficients of the five theorems are explicit functions of $k$, so equality in the model and the strict signs are computed from the displayed formulas. The only non-elementary point is the strict monotonicity of the model angle in $k$: differentiating the half-angle form of the model cosine law writes the derivative of the angle as a positive multiple of $\cos^2(\theta/2)G(u)+\sin^2(\theta/2)G(s)-G(v)$, where $G(t)=\operatorname{sn}_k(t)m_k(t)$ with $m_k(t)=\int_0^t x\operatorname{sn}_k(x)\,dx$, and this expression is positive because $t\mapsto G(t)$ is, as a function of $h=\operatorname{sn}_k^{\,2}$, a strictly convex function.

1.1 Elementary scalar estimates. [F3]
For $x>0$ one has $\sin x<x$: the function $x-\sin x$ vanishes at $0$ and has derivative $1-\cos x\ge0$, which is positive except at multiples of $2\pi$, so it is strictly increasing on $[0,2\pi]$ and then visibly positive; for $x>0$ one has $\sinh x>x$, since $\sinh x-x$ vanishes at $0$ and has derivative $\cosh x-1\ge0$, positive for $x>0$. For $0<x<\pi$ one has $\cot x<1/x$: for $0<x\le\pi/2$ the function $\sin x-x\cos x$ vanishes at $0$ and has derivative $x\sin x>0$, so $\sin x>x\cos x$ and $\cot x=\cos x/\sin x<1/x$; for $\pi/2<x<\pi$ one has $\cot x<0<1/x$. For $y>0$ one has $\coth y>1/y$: $y\cosh y-\sinh y$ vanishes at $0$ and has derivative $y\sinh y>0$, so $y\cosh y>\sinh y$ and $\coth y=\cosh y/\sinh y>1/y$. Also $\cos x\le1$ and $\cosh y\ge1$, with the latter inequality strict for $y>0$. [F3]

1.2 The model Jacobi field is strictly shorter at larger curvature. [F1, F2]
For fixed $t>0$ put $$m_k(t):=\int_0^t x\,\operatorname{sn}_k(x)\,dx .$$ Since $\operatorname{sn}_k>0$ on $(0,D_k)$, where $D_k:=\pi/\sqrt k$ for $k>0$ and $D_k:=+\infty$ for $k\le0$, one has $m_k(t)>0$ for $0<t<D_k$. From the explicit formulas, for $k\ne0$, $$\partial_k\operatorname{sn}_k(t)=\frac{t\operatorname{cs}_k(t)-\operatorname{sn}_k(t)}{2k}=-\frac{m_k(t)}{2},$$ the first equality following by differentiating the displayed quotient $\sin(\sqrt k\,t)/\sqrt k$ (respectively $\sinh(\sqrt{-k}\,t)/\sqrt{-k}$) in $k$, and the second from $t\operatorname{cs}_k-\operatorname{sn}_k=(t\operatorname{cs}_k-\operatorname{sn}_k)(0)+\int_0^t(-kx\operatorname{sn}_k(x))\,dx=-k\,m_k(t)$, which uses $(\operatorname{cs}_k)'=-k\operatorname{sn}_k$ [F2]. At $k=0$, [F11] gives $\operatorname{sn}_k(t)=t-kt^3/6+o(k)$ from either side, so $\partial_k\operatorname{sn}_k(t)|_{k=0}=-t^3/6=-m_0(t)/2$. The derivative formula extends continuously across $k=0$ since the explicit model functions converge uniformly on the finite interval $[0,t]$. Hence $\partial_k\operatorname{sn}_k(t)<0$: for fixed $t>0$ the function $k\mapsto\operatorname{sn}_k(t)$ is continuously differentiable and strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,\pi^2/t^2)$. In particular $\operatorname{sn}_k(t)<t$ for $0<k<\pi^2/t^2$, $\operatorname{sn}_0(t)=t$ and $\operatorname{sn}_k(t)>t$ for $k<0$; by [F5] the same comparison is the strict sign of the Rauch comparison between the space forms of curvatures $k_1<k_2$: for matched initial derivatives of the same norm $|E|>0$, one has $|J_{k_2}(t)|=\operatorname{sn}_{k_2}(t)|E|<\operatorname{sn}_{k_1}(t)|E|=|J_{k_1}(t)|$. If $E=0$, both fields are identically zero. [F1, F2, F5, F11, step 1.1]

1.3 The model cotangent is strictly smaller at larger curvature. [F1, F3]
From the explicit formulas, $\operatorname{ct}_0(t)=1/t$, $\operatorname{ct}_k(t)=\sqrt k\cot(\sqrt k\,t)$ for $k>0$ and $\operatorname{ct}_k(t)=\sqrt{-k}\coth(\sqrt{-k}\,t)$ for $k<0$, and $\operatorname{ct}_k(t)\to1/t$ as $k\to0$ in either sign. For $k>0$, with $x=\sqrt k\,t\in(0,\pi)$, $$\frac{d}{dk}\operatorname{ct}_k(t)=\frac{\sin x\cos x-x}{2\sqrt k\,\sin^2x}<0,$$ because $\sin x\cos x\le\sin x<x$ for $x>0$ by step 1.1 (for $x\le\pi/2$ use $\sin x<x$ and $\cos x\le1$; for $x>\pi/2$, $\sin x\cos x<0<x$). For $k<0$, with $y=\sqrt{-k}\,t>0$, $$\frac{d}{dk}\operatorname{ct}_k(t)=-\frac{\sinh y\cosh y-y}{2\sqrt{-k}\,\sinh^2y}<0,$$ because $y<\sinh y\cosh y$ by step 1.1 applied to $\sinh(2y)>2y$. Hence for fixed $t>0$ the function $k\mapsto\operatorname{ct}_k(t)$ is strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,\pi^2/t^2)$, and $\operatorname{ct}_k(t)<1/t$ for $k>0$, $=1/t$ for $k=0$, $>1/t$ for $k<0$. By [F8] this is exactly the strict sign of the Hessian and Laplacian comparisons between the model of curvature $k$ and the flat model: the curvature bound $K\ge k'$ holds in $M^n_k$ whenever $k\ge k'$ [F6, F7], and the attained model value $\operatorname{ct}_k$ is strictly below $\operatorname{ct}_{k'}$ when $k>k'$. [F1, F3, F6, F7, F8, step 1.1]

1.4 Equality in the constant-$k$ model. The five comparisons are equalities in $M^n_k$ and $M^2_k$:
- Jacobi: by [F5] the matched normal Jacobi field of the model is $J(t)=\operatorname{sn}_k(t)P_tE$, so the Rauch bound is attained at every $t$ of the domain.
- Hessian and Laplacian: by [F8], $\operatorname{Hess}r$ and $\Delta_gr$ equal the comparison expressions of [F6] and [F7] exactly, and the two curvature hypotheses hold with equality.
- Volume: by [F9], $\operatorname{vol}_g(B(p,r))=V^\star_k(r)$, so the Bishop–Gromov ratio is identically $1$.
- Toponogov: by [F4] a comparison triangle in $M^2_k$ is unique up to isometry, so the comparison triangle of an admissible model triangle is congruent to the triangle itself and every model angle equals its comparison angle; in the hinge form the model opposite side is by definition $c_k(a,b,\theta)$ [F10], so both comparisons hold with equality.
In each case the bounding quantity is exactly the model quantity, so no strictness remains inside a fixed model; strictness can only appear between models of different curvature, which is what steps 1.2, 1.3, 2.1 and 4.1 compute.
[F4, F5, F8, F9, F10]

1.5 The primitives $m$, $G$ and $\rho$. [F1]
For the rest of the computation fix $k$ and write $m(t):=m_k(t)=\int_0^t x\operatorname{sn}_k(x)\,dx$ on the positive domain, $h(t):=\operatorname{sn}_k(t)^2$, $G(t):=\operatorname{sn}_k(t)m(t)=h(t)\rho(t)$ with $\rho(t):=m(t)/\operatorname{sn}_k(t)$, and $\tan_k(t):=\operatorname{sn}_k(t)/\operatorname{cs}_k(t)$. Then $m(0)=0$, $m'=t\operatorname{sn}_k(t)$, $m$ is odd and $m>0$ on $(0,D_k)$; $h$ is even and strictly increasing on $(0,D_k/2)$ (for $k>0$ its restriction is $\sin^2(\sqrt k\,t)/k$, for $k\le0$ it is $t^2$ or $\sinh^2(\sqrt{-k}\,t)/(-k)$), with $h(t)>0$ for $0<t<D_k$; $G$ is even and $G>0$ on $(0,D_k)$; and on $(0,D_k/2)$ one has $\operatorname{cs}_k>0$, hence $\tan_k>0$. [F1]

1.6 Half-angle form of the model cosine law. [F3, F4]
Let $(a,b,c)$ be admissible with angle $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ opposite $c$ as in [F4], and put $s=(a+b)/2$, $u=(a-b)/2$, $v=c/2$. Then $$\sin^2\frac\theta2=\frac{h(v)-h(u)}{\operatorname{sn}_k(a)\operatorname{sn}_k(b)},\qquad \cos^2\frac\theta2=\frac{h(s)-h(v)}{\operatorname{sn}_k(a)\operatorname{sn}_k(b)},$$ and consequently the two identities $$h(s)-h(u)=\operatorname{sn}_k(a)\operatorname{sn}_k(b),\qquad h(v)=\cos^2\frac\theta2\,h(u)+\sin^2\frac\theta2\,h(s).$$ For $k\ne0$ this is a computation from the cosine law of [F4]: the addition formulas of [F3] give $\operatorname{cs}_k(a\pm b)=\operatorname{cs}_k(a)\operatorname{cs}_k(b)\mp k\operatorname{sn}_k(a)\operatorname{sn}_k(b)$, so $$1-\cos\theta=\frac{\operatorname{cs}_k(a-b)-\operatorname{cs}_k(c)}{k\operatorname{sn}_k(a)\operatorname{sn}_k(b)},\qquad 1+\cos\theta=\frac{\operatorname{cs}_k(c)-\operatorname{cs}_k(a+b)}{k\operatorname{sn}_k(a)\operatorname{sn}_k(b)},$$ and $\operatorname{cs}_k(2x)=1-2k\operatorname{sn}_k(x)^2$ converts the right hand sides into the two displayed expressions, whose sum is $1$ and gives the third identity; the fourth follows by substituting the third into the first. For $k=0$ the same identities are the elementary Euclidean computation: $\sin^2(\theta/2)=(v^2-u^2)/(ab)$, $\cos^2(\theta/2)=(s^2-v^2)/(ab)$, $s^2-u^2=ab$ and $v^2=\cos^2(\theta/2)u^2+\sin^2(\theta/2)s^2$ follow from $c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos\theta$. Also, the map $\theta\mapsto c_k(a,b,\theta)$ is strictly increasing on $(0,\pi)$: the first identity writes $h(c_k(a,b,\theta)/2)=h(u)+\operatorname{sn}_k(a)\operatorname{sn}_k(b)\sin^2(\theta/2)$ whose right-hand side varies strictly increasingly in $\theta$. For $k>0$ the model opposite side is less than $D_k$, so its half lies in $(0,D_k/2)$, where $h$ is strictly increasing; for $k\le0$ the same holds for every positive half-side. Hence $c_k(a,b,\theta)$ and $\theta$ determine each other strictly increasingly. [F3, F4, step 1.5]

1.7 The ratio $\rho$ is strictly increasing.

1.8 The five strict signs and their directions.
In the three cases, using the explicit forms of $\operatorname{sn}_k$ and the identity $m(t)=(\operatorname{sn}_k(t)-t\operatorname{cs}_k(t))/k$ for $k\ne0$ (both sides vanish at $0$ and have derivative $t\operatorname{sn}_k(t)$):
- $k>0$: with $x=\sqrt k\,t$, $\rho(t)=(1-x\cot x)/k$ and $\rho'(t)=(x-\sin x\cos x)/(\sqrt k\,\sin^2x)>0$ by step 1.1;
- $k=0$: $\rho(t)=t^2/3$, so $\rho'(t)=2t/3>0$;
- $k<0$: with $y=\sqrt{-k}\,t$, $\rho(t)=(y\coth y-1)/(-k)$ and $\rho'(t)=(\sinh y\cosh y-y)/(\sqrt{-k}\,\sinh^2y)>0$ by step 1.1.
Thus $\rho$ is strictly increasing on $(0,D_k)$. No monotonicity of $G=h\rho$ on the whole positive domain is asserted.
[F1, F3, step 1.1, step 1.5]

1.9 Audit of hypotheses, degenerate cases and choice.
For all $a,b>0$, with $s=(a+b)/2$ and $u=(a-b)/2$, $$\operatorname{sn}_k(u)m(u)+\tfrac12\bigl[m(a)\operatorname{sn}_k(b)+\operatorname{sn}_k(a)m(b)\bigr]=\operatorname{sn}_k(s)m(s).$$ For $k\ne0$, multiply the difference of the two sides by $k$ and use $m(t)=(\operatorname{sn}_k(t)-t\operatorname{cs}_k(t))/k$ together with the product-to-sum consequences of [F3]: $\operatorname{sn}_k(x)\operatorname{cs}_k(x)=\operatorname{sn}_k(2x)/2$, $\operatorname{sn}_k(x)\operatorname{sn}_k(y)=(\operatorname{cs}_k(x-y)-\operatorname{cs}_k(x+y))/(2k)$, $\operatorname{cs}_k(x)\operatorname{cs}_k(y)=(\operatorname{cs}_k(x-y)+\operatorname{cs}_k(x+y))/2$, $\operatorname{sn}_k(x)\operatorname{cs}_k(y)=(\operatorname{sn}_k(x+y)+\operatorname{sn}_k(x-y))/2$; then the difference equals $$\bigl[h(u)-h(s)+\operatorname{sn}_k(a)\operatorname{sn}_k(b)\bigr] +\Bigl[-\tfrac{u}{2}\operatorname{sn}_k(2u)-\tfrac12\bigl(a\operatorname{cs}_k(a)\operatorname{sn}_k(b)+b\operatorname{sn}_k(a)\operatorname{cs}_k(b)\bigr)+\tfrac{s}{2}\operatorname{sn}_k(2s)\Bigr],$$ whose first bracket is zero by the addition formula for $\operatorname{cs}_k(2\cdot)$ and whose second bracket is zero because $a\operatorname{cs}_k(a)\operatorname{sn}_k(b)+b\operatorname{sn}_k(a)\operatorname{cs}_k(b)=s\operatorname{sn}_k(2s)-u\operatorname{sn}_k(2u)$; hence the difference is zero. For $k=0$ the identity reads $u^4/3+(a^3b+ab^3)/6=s^4/3$ and follows from $s^4-u^4=(s-u)(s+u)(s^2+u^2)=ab(a^2+b^2)/2$. [F2, F3, step 1.5]

2.1 The saturated model volume is strictly smaller at larger curvature. [F1, F9, step 1.2] For $k_1<k_2$, put $D_i:=D_{k_i}$, with $D_i=+\infty$ when $k_i\le0$. Then $D_2\le D_1$, and step 1.2 gives $A_{k_2}(t)<A_{k_1}(t)$ for $0<t<D_2$. For every $r>0$, $$V^\star_{k_i}(r)=\int_0^{\min\{r,D_i\}}A_{k_i}(t)\,dt.$$ The $k_1$ integral covers at least $(0,\min\{r,D_2\})$, on which its density is strictly larger. Hence $$V^\star_{k_2}(r)<V^\star_{k_1}(r)\qquad(r>0).$$ Thus the larger-curvature model has strictly smaller saturated balls, the strict form of the flat-versus-curved Bishop–Gromov comparison. [F1, F9, step 1.2]
Let $\Gamma$ be defined on the set of values of $h$ by $\Gamma(h(t)):=G(t)$ for $t\in(0,D_k/2)$; this is well defined because $h$ is a strictly increasing bijection from $(0,D_k/2)$ onto its image. The formulas $G(t)\to0$ and $h(t)\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$ extend $\Gamma$ continuously by $\Gamma(0)=0$; when $k>0$, the explicit model formulas likewise extend it continuously to $h(D_k/2)$. Then $$\frac{d\Gamma}{dh}=\frac{\rho(t)}2+\frac{t}2\tan_k(t),\qquad \frac{d^2\Gamma}{dh^2}=\frac{\rho'(t)+\tan_k(t)+t/\operatorname{cs}_k(t)^2}{4\operatorname{sn}_k(t)\operatorname{cs}_k(t)}>0$$ at $h=h(t)$, $t\in(0,D_k/2)$. Indeed, $dh/dt=2\operatorname{sn}_k\operatorname{cs}_k$ and $dG/dt=\operatorname{cs}_k\,m+\operatorname{sn}_k\,m'=\operatorname{sn}_k(\operatorname{cs}_k\rho+t\operatorname{sn}_k)$, so $\frac{d\Gamma}{dh}=(dG/dt)/(dh/dt)=\rho/2+(t/2)\tan_k$; differentiating the last expression with respect to $t$ and dividing by $2\operatorname{sn}_k\operatorname{cs}_k$ gives the displayed second derivative, whose numerator is positive because $\rho'>0$ (step 1.7), $\tan_k>0$, $t>0$ and $\operatorname{sn}_k,\operatorname{cs}_k>0$ on $(0,D_k/2)$, while $(\tan_k)'=(1+k\tan_k^2)=\operatorname{cs}_k^{-2}$ by the Wronskian identity [F2]. Hence $\Gamma$ is strictly convex on the interior and, by its continuous endpoint extension, on every closed subinterval of the extended domain. [F2, step 1.5, step 1.7]

2.2 The addition identity for $G$. [F2, F3, step 1.5]
Let $(a,b,c)$ be admissible, $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ its angle at the vertex between the sides $a$ and $b$, and set $$M_1:=\cos^2\frac\theta2\,G(u)+\sin^2\frac\theta2\,G(s)-G(v), \qquad s=\frac{a+b}2,\quad u=\frac{a-b}2,\quad v=\frac c2 .$$ Then $M_1>0$. To see this, put $t_s:=s$ if $k\le0$ or $s\le D_k/2$, and $t_s:=D_k-s$ if $k>0$ and $s>D_k/2$. Then $t_s\in(0,D_k/2]$ and $h(t_s)=h(s)$. Also $|u|<v<t_s$: when $t_s=s$ this follows from the strict triangle inequality, and when $s>D_k/2$ it follows from $a+b+c<2D_k$. Since $\rho$ is strictly increasing and $h(s)=h(t_s)>0$, $G(t_s)\le G(s)$, strictly if $t_s<s$. Thus $|u|<v<t_s\le D_k/2$, and $h(u),h(v),h(t_s)$ lie in the increasing range of $h$; the fourth identity of step 1.6 makes $h(v)$ a strict convex combination of $h(u)$ and $h(t_s)$ with weights $\cos^2(\theta/2)$ and $\sin^2(\theta/2)$, both in $(0,1)$. Strict convexity of $\Gamma$ (step 2.3) on the closed interval between $h(u)$ and $h(t_s)$ gives $$G(v)=\Gamma(h(v))<\cos^2\tfrac\theta2\,\Gamma(h(u))+\sin^2\tfrac\theta2\,\Gamma(h(t_s)) =\cos^2\tfrac\theta2\,G(u)+\sin^2\tfrac\theta2\,G(t_s)\le\cos^2\tfrac\theta2\,G(u)+\sin^2\tfrac\theta2\,G(s),$$ so $M_1>0$; here $G(u)=G(|u|)$ because $G$ is even. This is the only place where the saturation $s>D_k/2$ of the positive-curvature model is handled. [step 1.5, step 1.6, step 1.7, step 2.2, step 2.3]

2.3 The conjugate function $\Gamma$ is strictly convex. [F2, step 1.7, step 1.5]
Fix an admissible side datum $(a,b,c)$ and let $\theta(k)$ be the model angle opposite $c$ between the sides $a$ and $b$ in $M^2_k$, as $k$ ranges over the open admissible interval $(-\infty,k_{\max})$ (where $k_{\max}:=\min\{(\pi/\max\{a,b,c\})^2,(2\pi/(a+b+c))^2\}$); on this interval the datum stays nondegenerate and $\theta(k)\in(0,\pi)$. Then $$\theta'(k)=\frac{2M_1(k)}{\operatorname{sn}_k(a)\operatorname{sn}_k(b)\sin\theta(k)}>0,$$ where $M_1(k)$ is the positive quantity of step 3.1 computed with the model functions at $k$. Indeed, differentiating the fourth identity of step 1.6 in $k$ gives $$-G(v)=\frac{d}{dk}\Bigl[\cos^2\tfrac\theta2\Bigr](h(u)-h(s))-\cos^2\tfrac\theta2\,G(u)-\sin^2\tfrac\theta2\,G(s),$$ because at each fixed argument $t$, $\partial_k h(t)=2\operatorname{sn}_k(t)\partial_k\operatorname{sn}_k(t)=-G(t)$ by step 1.2; since $\frac{d}{dk}\cos^2(\theta/2)=-\tfrac12\sin\theta\,\theta'$ and $h(u)-h(s)=-\operatorname{sn}_k(a)\operatorname{sn}_k(b)$ by step 1.6, this rearranges to the displayed formula. Its right-hand side is positive because $M_1(k)>0$, $\operatorname{sn}_k(a),\operatorname{sn}_k(b)>0$ (the datum is admissible at $k$) and $\sin\theta(k)>0$. Therefore $\theta$ is strictly increasing on the admissible interval: for $k_1<k_2$ with the datum admissible at both, $\alpha_{k_2}(a,b,c)=\theta(k_2)>\theta(k_1)=\alpha_{k_1}(a,b,c)$. For fixed $\theta\in(0,\pi)$, if $c_{k_2}(a,b,\theta)\ge c_{k_1}(a,b,\theta)$, strict increase of the angle at fixed side lengths in $k$ and of the model side at fixed $k$ in $\theta$ would give an angle greater than $\theta$ at $k_2$ for its own side length, a contradiction. Thus $c_{k_2}(a,b,\theta)<c_{k_1}(a,b,\theta)$. [F1, F4, step 1.2, step 1.6, step 3.1]

3.1 The half-angle numerator is positive. [step 1.5, step 1.6, step 1.7, step 2.2, step 2.3]
Assemble the computations. For $k_1<k_2$ with the relevant data admissible at both curvatures:
- Rauch: for matched initial derivatives with common norm $|E|>0$, the model Jacobi field at $k_2$ is strictly shorter than at $k_1$ at every positive time in their common domain (step 1.2); in particular, against the flat model, positive curvature gives strictly shorter fields and negative curvature strictly longer fields, while inside a fixed model the bound is an equality (step 1.4). This is consistent with [F5]: in $M^n_{k_2}$ one has $\sec=k_2\ge k_1$, so Rauch's inequality $|J_{k_2}|\le|J_{k_1}|$ is strict for $E\ne0$; for $E=0$ both sides are zero.
- Hessian and Laplacian: $\operatorname{ct}_{k_2}(t)<\operatorname{ct}_{k_1}(t)$ for $t>0$ in the common domain (step 1.3), so the space-form values $\operatorname{ct}_k$ of [F8] give strict inequalities relative to the comparison values of [F6], [F7]: the flat-versus-positive sign is $\operatorname{ct}_k(t)<1/t$ and the flat-versus-negative sign is $\operatorname{ct}_k(t)>1/t$. The directions match $\operatorname{Hess}r\le\operatorname{ct}_k\,g$ and $\Delta_gr\le(n-1)\operatorname{ct}_k$ under $K\ge k$, $\operatorname{Ric}\ge(n-1)k\,g$.
- Volume: $V^\star_{k_2}(r)<V^\star_{k_1}(r)$ for every $r>0$ (step 2.1): the model of larger curvature has strictly smaller balls, matching the Bishop–Gromov upper bound, with equality inside a fixed model (step 1.4).
- Toponogov: $\alpha_{k_2}>\alpha_{k_1}$ and $c_{k_2}(a,b,\theta)<c_{k_1}(a,b,\theta)$ for nondegenerate data (step 4.1): the model of larger curvature has strictly fatter triangles and strictly shorter opposite sides, matching the hinge inequality $c\le c_k(a,b,\theta)$ and the angle inequality $\alpha\ge\bar\alpha$ under $K\ge k$ [F10], with equality inside a fixed model (step 1.4).
All equalities inside a fixed model are those of step 1.4. The example is a direction diagnostic only: every statement above is about the explicitly displayed model functions, no item of either page lists this example among its dependencies, and no later proof uses it.
[F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 1.4, step 4.1]

4.1 The model angle is strictly increasing in the curvature. [F1, F4, step 1.2, step 1.6, step 3.1]
The zero initial derivative $E=0$ gives the zero Jacobi field at every curvature; it retains model equality and is excluded only from the strict field comparison. The strict monotonicity of step 4.1 is asserted for nondegenerate admissible data only: $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ and the strict triangle inequalities are used through the hypothesis $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ and through $|u|<v$, and the degenerate limits $\theta=0$ and $\theta=\pi$ are excluded, in agreement with the admissibility convention of [F4] and the strict inequalities of [F10]. The boundary case $k=0$ is treated throughout: the model functions have their $k=0$ values, the half-angle identities of step 1.6 reduce to the Euclidean cosine law and are proved there directly, the primitive $m$ is $t^3/3$ and the addition identity of step 2.2 is proved separately for $k=0$; the formula of step 4.1 uses only the identity of step 1.6, not a division by $k$. The case $s>D_k/2$ of the positive-curvature model, where the sine is decreasing in its argument, is handled in step 3.1 through the reflection $t_s=D_k-s$; for $k\le0$ no such case occurs since $D_k=+\infty$. The isosceles case $a=b$, i.e. $u=0$, is included: then $h(u)=0$ and the strict convexity inequality of step 3.1 still separates $h(u)$ from $h(s)$ because $s>0$. The endpoint radius and time values of the comparison theorems ($p$, the cut locus, $r=0$, $t_0=\pi/\sqrt k$) are excluded exactly as in [F6]–[F9] and are never substituted into a formula; the saturated model volume $V^\star_k$ handles $r\ge\pi/\sqrt k$ without evaluating the density at the spherical endpoint. No family of objects is selected: the model geodesics, triangles and Jacobi fields are supplied by the cited model definitions, so the inherited $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [A1] suffices and no further choice is used. No converse implication is asserted and no statement of this example is used by any other item; the diagnostic claims of steps 1.5 and 1.8 are consistent with, and independent of, the comparison theorems they test.
[A1, F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.4, step 1.5, step 1.6, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎



The equality case and the model computations are classical: the model solutions $\operatorname{sn}_k,\operatorname{cs}_k,\operatorname{ct}_k$ and their comparison roles are Datar, *Lectures on Riemannian Geometry*, §24.1 (printed pp.173–176) and Eschenburg, *Comparison Theorems in Riemannian Geometry*, §2 (printed pp.6–11); the space-form equalities in the Hessian, Laplacian and volume comparisons are Eschenburg §§3–5 (printed pp.11–20) and Datar §§26–27; the Toponogov comparison with its equality case in constant curvature is Eschenburg §6 (printed pp.21–25) and Lang, Chapter 5, Theorem 5.15 (printed pp.70–71, PDF pp.73–74). The half-angle law of cosines used in step 1.6 is Lang, *Riemannian and Metric Geometry*, Chapter 5, Lemma 5.1, and the strict monotonicity of the model opposite side in the included angle used there is the same chapter's Lemma 5.2 (printed pp.64–65); the strict monotonicity of the model angle in the curvature proved in step 4.1 is the classical comparison quantity monotonicity that underlies the space-form ordering, and it is derived here from the displayed formulas rather than quoted.

**Given:** The integers $n\ge2$, the real number $a>0$, the open half-space $U^n=\{y>0\}$ with its global coordinates $x^1,\dots,x^{n-1},y$, the metric $g_a$, and the inherited $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [A1].

[A1] The countable-choice premise is the inherited $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), inherited through the sectional-curvature interface [F3], geodesic existence and uniqueness [F4], and the Hopf–Rinow equivalence [F5]; the metric, the geodesics and the model functions below are explicit and no family is selected.

[F1] Coordinate criterion for Riemannian metrics ([[prop-coordinate-criterion-for-a-riemannian-metric]]): a tensor field $g=\sum_{i,j}g_{ij}\,dx^i\otimes dx^j$ with smooth symmetric coefficients is a Riemannian metric exactly when the matrix $(g_{ij})$ is positive definite at every point, and under a change of coordinates $J=\partial x/\partial\xi$ the matrices transform by $G_\xi=J^{\mathsf T}G_xJ$.

[F2] Christoffel symbols and geodesics ([[prop-christoffel-formula-for-the-levi-civita-connection]], [[prop-coordinate-geodesic-equation]]): the Levi-Civita symbols are $$\Gamma^k{}_{ij}=\tfrac12 g^{kl}\bigl(\partial_i g_{jl}+\partial_j g_{il}-\partial_l g_{ij}\bigr),$$ and a smooth curve is a geodesic exactly when its coordinate expression satisfies $\ddot x^k+\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\dot x^i\dot x^j=0$ in every chart.

[F3] Curvature in coordinates ([[prop-coordinate-formula-for-the-curvature-tensor]], [[thm-curvature-is-a-type-one-three-tensor]], [[def-riemann-curvature-four-tensor]], [[def-sectional-curvature]]): with the page convention, $$R^\ell{}_{kij}=\partial_i\Gamma^\ell{}_{jk}-\partial_j\Gamma^\ell{}_{ik} +\Gamma^m{}_{jk}\Gamma^\ell{}_{im}-\Gamma^m{}_{ik}\Gamma^\ell{}_{jm},$$ the curvature is a smooth tensor, so an identity proved on coordinate frames extends multilinearly; $\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W)=g(R(X,Y)Z,W)$; and the sectional curvature of an independent pair $(u,v)$ is $\operatorname{Rm}(u,v,v,u)$ divided by the positive Gram determinant $g(u,u)g(v,v)-g(u,v)^2$.

[F4] Geodesics are unique and affinely reparametrizable ([[thm-existence-uniqueness-and-smooth-dependence-of-geodesics]], [[prop-affine-reparametrization-of-a-geodesic-is-a-geodesic]]): for every initial datum $(p,v)$ there is a unique maximal geodesic, smooth in its arguments; an affine reparametrization $t\mapsto ct+d$, $c\ne0$, of a geodesic is a geodesic.

[F5] Hopf–Rinow ([[thm-hopf-rinow]]): for a nonempty connected boundaryless Riemannian manifold, geodesic completeness and metric completeness are equivalent; in particular a Riemannian manifold on which every maximal geodesic is defined on all of $\mathbb R$ is a complete metric space.

[F6] Hyperbolic functions ([[def-hyperbolic-functions]], [[thm-hyperbolic-identities-and-derivatives]]): $\operatorname{sech}=1/\cosh$, $\tanh=\sinh/\cosh$, $\cosh^2-\sinh^2=1$, $(\tanh)'=\operatorname{sech}^2$ and $(\operatorname{sech})'=-\operatorname{sech}\tanh$; dividing the Pythagorean identity by $\cosh^2$ gives $\operatorname{sech}^2+\tanh^2=1$ as well.

[F7] Convexity and simple connectivity ([[cor-convex-subsets-of-rn-are-contractible]], [[cor-contractible-spaces-are-path-connected]], [[lem-contractibility-implies-trivial-fundamental-group]], [[def-simply-connected]], [[thm-path-connected-implies-connected]]): the open half-space $U^n$ is convex, hence contractible and path connected, and its fundamental group at every basepoint is trivial; a nonempty path connected space with trivial fundamental group is simply connected, and a path connected space is connected.



1.1 The metric $g_a$ is Riemannian and $U^n$ is boundaryless. [F1, given]
In the global coordinates $g_{ij}=(a^2y^2)^{-1}\delta_{ij}$ is smooth and symmetric, and for $v\ne0$ $$g_a(v,v)=\frac{1}{a^2y^2}\sum_i(v^i)^2>0$$ because $y>0$. The coordinate criterion [F1] therefore makes $g_a$ a Riemannian metric on the open set $U^n$, which is an $n$-dimensional boundaryless smooth manifold as an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$. [F1, given]

1.2 Every maximal geodesic is one of these and is defined for all time.
Write $f=(ay)^{-1}$, so that $g_{ij}=f^2\delta_{ij}$, and put $f_l:=\partial_l f$; since $f$ depends only on $y=x^n$ one has $f_l=f'\delta_{ln}$ with $f'=-1/(ay^2)=-f/y$. Substituting $\partial_l g_{ij}=2ff_l\delta_{ij}$ and $g^{kl}=f^{-2}\delta^{kl}$ in the formula of [F2] gives $$\Gamma^k{}_{ij}=f^{-1}\delta^{kl}\bigl(f_i\delta_{jl}+f_j\delta_{il}-f_l\delta_{ij}\bigr) =\frac{f'}{f}\bigl(\delta_{in}\delta^k_{\ j}+\delta_{jn}\delta^k_{\ i} -\delta^k_{\ n}\delta_{ij}\bigr) =-\frac{1}{y}\bigl(\delta_{in}\delta^k_{\ j}+\delta_{jn}\delta^k_{\ i} -\delta_{kn}\delta_{ij}\bigr),$$ where the second equality contracts $\delta^{kl}f'\delta_{ln}=f'\delta^k_n$ in each of the three terms and the third uses $f'/f=-y^{-1}$ and $\delta^k_{\ n}=\delta_{kn}$. The symbols depend on the point only through the factor $y^{-1}$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

1.3 Simple connectedness and the boundary cases.
Put $\varepsilon_i:=\delta_{in}$ and $$A^\ell{}_{jk}:=\varepsilon_j\delta^\ell_{\ k}+\varepsilon_k\delta^\ell_{\ j} -\delta_{jk}\varepsilon^\ell,$$ so that step 2.1 reads $\Gamma^\ell{}_{jk}=-y^{-1}A^\ell{}_{jk}$ and $\partial_i\Gamma^\ell{}_{jk}=y^{-2}\varepsilon_iA^\ell{}_{jk}$. Substitution in the coordinate formula of [F3] gives $$\partial_i\Gamma^\ell{}_{jk}-\partial_j\Gamma^\ell{}_{ik} =y^{-2}\bigl(\varepsilon_iA^\ell{}_{jk}-\varepsilon_jA^\ell{}_{ik}\bigr) =y^{-2}\bigl(\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_k\delta^\ell_{\ j} -\varepsilon_j\varepsilon_k\delta^\ell_{\ i} -\varepsilon_i\varepsilon^\ell\delta_{jk} +\varepsilon_j\varepsilon^\ell\delta_{ik}\bigr),$$ the second equality expanding the two $A$'s and cancelling the two terms $\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_j\delta^\ell_{\ k}$. Expanding the two quadratic terms likewise gives $$\Gamma^m{}_{jk}\Gamma^\ell{}_{im}-\Gamma^m{}_{ik}\Gamma^\ell{}_{jm} =y^{-2}\bigl(A^m{}_{jk}A^\ell{}_{im}-A^m{}_{ik}A^\ell{}_{jm}\bigr) =y^{-2}\bigl(\delta_{ik}\delta^\ell_{\ j}-\delta_{jk}\delta^\ell_{\ i} -\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_k\delta^\ell_{\ j} +\varepsilon_j\varepsilon_k\delta^\ell_{\ i} +\varepsilon_i\varepsilon^\ell\delta_{jk} -\varepsilon_j\varepsilon^\ell\delta_{ik}\bigr),$$ so that the four $\varepsilon$-terms of the quadratic expansion are exactly the negatives of the four $\varepsilon$-terms of the derivative expansion and cancel them, leaving $$R^\ell{}_{kij}=y^{-2}\bigl(\delta_{ik}\delta^\ell_{\ j} -\delta_{jk}\delta^\ell_{\ i}\bigr).$$ Since $g_{ik}=f^2\delta_{ik}$ with $f^{-2}=a^2y^2$, this is $$R(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_k =y^{-2}\bigl(\delta_{ik}\partial_j-\delta_{jk}\partial_i\bigr) =-a^2\bigl(g_{jk}\partial_i-g_{ik}\partial_j\bigr).$$ Tensoriality of $R$ in [F3] upgrades this identity on coordinate frames to $$R(X,Y)Z=-a^2\bigl(g(Y,Z)X-g(X,Z)Y\bigr)$$ for arbitrary tangent vectors. Pairing with $X=u$ after putting $Y=Z=v$ and using [F3] gives $$\operatorname{Rm}(u,v,v,u)=-a^2\bigl(g(u,u)g(v,v)-g(u,v)^2\bigr),$$ so for a basis $(u,v)$ of any tangent two-plane the positive Gram determinant in the denominator cancels and the sectional curvature is $K=-a^2$ at every point of $U^n$. [F2, F3, step 2.1]

2.1 The Christoffel symbols. [F1, F2, step 1.1]
Let $x_0\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and $y_0>0$, and put $\gamma(t)=(x_0,y_0e^{at})$. Then $\gamma$ is smooth, takes values in $U^n$ and is defined on all of $\mathbb R$. Its coordinates are $\gamma^i=x_0^i$ for $i<n$ and $\gamma^n=y_0e^{at}=:y(t)$, so $\dot\gamma^i=0$ for $i<n$ and $\dot\gamma^n=ay$, and $\ddot\gamma^i=0$ for $i<n$, $\ddot\gamma^n=a^2y$. Substituting the symbols of step 2.1, for $k<n$ every term contains the factor $\delta^k_{\ j}$ or $\delta^k_{\ i}$ or $\delta_{kn}$ with $k<n$, so $$\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\dot\gamma^i\dot\gamma^j =-\frac{1}{y}\bigl(\delta_{in}\delta^k_{\ j}+\delta_{jn}\delta^k_{\ i} -\delta_{kn}\delta_{ij}\bigr)\dot\gamma^i\dot\gamma^j=0,$$ while for $k=n$ the bracket is $\dot\gamma^n\dot\gamma^n+\dot\gamma^n\dot\gamma^n-|\dot\gamma|^2_{\mathrm E}=\dot y^2$, so $$\ddot\gamma^n+\Gamma^n{}_{ij}\dot\gamma^i\dot\gamma^j =a^2y-\frac{1}{y}\dot y^2=a^2y-\frac{1}{y}(ay)^2=0 .$$ Hence the geodesic equation of [F2] holds, and $\gamma$ is a geodesic defined on all of $\mathbb R$, of constant speed $g_a(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=(a^2y^2)^{-1}(ay)^2=1$. [F2, F4, F6, step 2.1]

3.1 The curvature tensor and the sectional curvature $-a^2$. [F2, F3, step 2.1]
By a horizontal translation and rotation it suffices to take $\bar c=0$ and $u=e_1$. Put $$\gamma(t)=\bigl(-\rho\tanh(at),\,0,\dots,0,\,\rho\operatorname{sech}(at)\bigr), \qquad y(t)=\rho\operatorname{sech}(at)>0 .$$ Then $\gamma$ takes values in $U^n$; by [F6] it is smooth and defined on all of $\mathbb R$, with $\dot\gamma^1(t)=-\rho a\operatorname{sech}^2(at)$, $\dot\gamma^n(t)=-\rho a\operatorname{sech}(at)\tanh(at)$ and all other components zero. Its acceleration is $\ddot\gamma^1=2\rho a^2\operatorname{sech}^2(at)\tanh(at)$ and $\ddot\gamma^n=\rho a^2\bigl(\operatorname{sech}(at)\tanh^2(at) -\operatorname{sech}^3(at)\bigr)$. By step 2.1 the only nonvanishing symbols with the present velocity are $\Gamma^1{}_{1n}=\Gamma^1{}_{n1}=-1/y$, $\Gamma^n{}_{11}=1/y$ and $\Gamma^n{}_{nn}=-1/y$; the remaining coordinates are constant with vanishing Christoffel contributions, since $A^k{}_{ij}=0$ whenever $k\ne n$ and both $i,j\ne n$. The $x^1$-component of the geodesic equation is therefore $$\ddot\gamma^1-\frac{2}{y}\dot\gamma^1\dot\gamma^n =2\rho a^2\operatorname{sech}^2\tanh -\frac{2\rho^2a^2\operatorname{sech}^3\tanh}{\rho\operatorname{sech}}=0,$$ and the $y$-component is $$\ddot\gamma^n-\frac{1}{y}\bigl((\dot\gamma^n)^2-(\dot\gamma^1)^2\bigr) =\rho a^2\operatorname{sech}\bigl(\tanh^2-\operatorname{sech}^2\bigr) -\frac{\rho^2a^2\operatorname{sech}^2\bigl(\tanh^2-\operatorname{sech}^2\bigr)}{\rho\operatorname{sech}}=0,$$ where the two displays use $\dot\gamma^1=-\rho a\operatorname{sech}^2$, $\dot\gamma^n=-\rho a\operatorname{sech}\tanh$ and $y=\rho\operatorname{sech}$. Hence $\gamma$ satisfies the geodesic equation and is a geodesic defined on all of $\mathbb R$, of constant $g_a$-speed $1$, because $$g_a(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma) =\frac{\rho^2a^2\operatorname{sech}^2(\operatorname{sech}^2+\tanh^2)} {a^2\rho^2\operatorname{sech}^2}=1$$ by the identity $\operatorname{sech}^2+\tanh^2=1$ of [F6]. [F2, F4, F6, step 2.1]

3.2 The vertical lines are complete geodesics. [F2, F4, F6, step 2.1]
Let $p=(\bar x_0,y_0)\in U^n$ and let $v\in T_pU^n$ be a unit vector with respect to $g_a$, decomposed as $v=(v_H,v_n)$ with $v_H\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and $v_n\in\mathbb R$, so that $|v_H|^2+v_n^2=a^2y_0^2$.
If $v_H=0$, then $v=\pm ay_0\partial_n$; the vertical line of step 3.2 passes through $p$ with velocity $ay_0\partial_n$ at $t=0$, and its time reversal $t\mapsto\gamma(-t)$ (an affine reparametrization, [F4]) passes through $p$ with velocity $-ay_0\partial_n$. So in this case the maximal geodesic with initial datum $(p,v)$ is that line, and its domain is $\mathbb R$.
Otherwise $v_H\ne0$. Put $u:=-v_H/|v_H|$, let $s\in\mathbb R$ be the unique solution of $\sinh s=-v_n/|v_H|$ (unique because $\sinh$ is strictly increasing and onto, [F6]), and set $$\rho:=y_0\cosh s>0,\qquad \bar c:=\bar x_0+\rho\tanh(s)\,u .$$ Consider the semicircle of step 3.3 with data $(\bar c,u,\rho)$: $$\gamma(t)=\bigl(\bar c-\rho\tanh(at)\,u,\ \rho\operatorname{sech}(at)\bigr) =:(\gamma_H(t),\gamma^n(t)).$$ At $t_1:=s/a$ its height is $\gamma^n(t_1)=\rho\operatorname{sech}s=y_0\cosh s\operatorname{sech}s=y_0$, so its horizontal part is $\bar c-\rho\tanh(s)u=\bar x_0$, that is, $\gamma(t_1)=p$. Its velocity there is $$\dot\gamma(t_1) =a y_0\bigl(-\operatorname{sech}(s)\,u,\ -\tanh(s)\bigr),$$ because $\rho a\operatorname{sech}^2s=ay_0\operatorname{sech}s$ and $\rho a\operatorname{sech}s\tanh s=ay_0\tanh s$. The identities $\cosh^2s=1+\sinh^2s$ and $\sinh s=-v_n/|v_H|$ give $$|v_H|=ay_0\operatorname{sech}s,\qquad v_n=-|v_H|\sinh s=-ay_0\tanh s,$$ using $\tanh s\cosh s=\sinh s$; together with $u=-v_H/|v_H|$ this shows $\dot\gamma(t_1)=(v_H,v_n)=v$. Hence the parameter-translated curve $t\mapsto\gamma(t+t_1)$ is a geodesic defined on all of $\mathbb R$ with initial datum $(p,v)$, so by uniqueness in [F4] it is the maximal geodesic of that initial datum, and its domain is $\mathbb R$.
For an arbitrary nonzero initial velocity $w$, apply the preceding
construction to $v=w/|w|_{g_a}$ and reparametrize by $t\mapsto |w|_{g_a}t$;
this gives a geodesic on $\mathbb R$ with velocity $w$, which is maximal by
uniqueness. For zero initial velocity the constant curve solves [F2] on
$\mathbb R$ and is maximal by [F4]. Thus every maximal geodesic of
$(U^n,g_a)$ has domain $\mathbb R$: the manifold is geodesically complete, and by Hopf–Rinow [F5] it is a complete metric space.
[F4, F5, F6, step 3.2, step 3.3]

3.3 The semicircles are complete geodesics. [F2, F4, F6, step 2.1]
The half-space $U^n=\{y>0\}$ is convex: for $x,z\in U^n$ and $t\in[0,1]$ the point $(1-t)x+tz$ has last coordinate $(1-t)x^n+tz^n>0$. Hence $U^n$ is contractible by [F7], so its fundamental group is trivial at every basepoint and it is path connected; by [F7] it is simply connected and connected. Together with completeness from step 1.2 and constant curvature $-a^2$ from step 3.1, $(U^n,g_a)$ is a complete, simply connected space form of curvature $k=-a^2$.
Boundary cases: the degenerate scale $a=0$ is excluded by hypothesis, since $g_0$ is not defined; the limiting boundary hyperplane $y=0$ is not part of $U^n$, and every geodesic of steps 3.2 and 3.3 is finite at every finite time but approaches the boundary only as $t\to\pm\infty$; the case $n=2$ exhibits the semicircles as the only nonvertical geodesics, and for $n>2$ each nonvertical geodesic lies in a two-plane spanned by its initial horizontal direction and $\partial_n$ while the remaining horizontal coordinates stay constant. Every geodesic in steps 3.2 and 3.3 is defined for all real times, so no endpoint of a maximal geodesic is finite. The only choice used is the inherited $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [A1], inherited through sectional curvature in step 3.1, geodesic existence and uniqueness in step 1.2, and Hopf–Rinow in step 1.2; the charts, the geodesics and the reparametrizations are explicit.
[F5, F7, step 1.2] ∎
